intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that auriculocondylar syndrome-4 (ARCND4) is caused by a tandem duplication on chromosome 7p21.1 that covers most of the HDAC9 gene (606543) and lies telomeric to TWIST1.

paragraphs.text: Auriculocondylar syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder of the first and second pharyngeal arches. Its features are malformed 'question mark' ears, prominent cheeks, microstomia, an abnormal temporomandibular joint, and hypoplasia of the mandibular condyle. Penetrance appears to be complete, but the features vary widely within and between families (Masotti et al., 2008). ARCND4 is caused by a 430-kb duplication that covers most of the HDAC9 gene and includes TWIST1 regulatory elements (Romanelli Tavares et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Masotti et al. (2008) described a multigeneration family (F1) with 11 individuals affected by auriculocondylar syndrome. The family showed variable clinical features. Many of the patients had facial asymmetry, a feature that the authors noted had not been highlighted in other reports of the syndrome.

checks.evidence_quote: We herein describe a new multigeneration family with 11 affected individuals (F1)

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) restudied the same family (F1), which was Brazilian and nonconsanguineous and included 11 members with typical features of ARCND. Among the members whose features were documented, 8 of 10 had question mark ears, 8 of 10 had microstomia, and 6 of 10 had micrognathia. Large, open fontanelles were not present. The features varied considerably within the family.

paragraphs.text: Masotti et al. (2008) reported autosomal dominant inheritance of auriculocondylar syndrome in the multigeneration family F1. In the same family, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) showed that the causal duplication segregated with the phenotype. Because all unaffected family members lacked the duplication, they suggested that penetrance was full.

checks.evidence_quote: Auriculo-condylar syndrome (ACS), an autosomal dominant disorder of first and second pharyngeal arches

paragraphs.text: Masotti et al. (2008) performed genome-wide linkage analysis in 2 large families with auriculocondylar syndrome. One family (F2) showed linkage to 1p21.1-q23.3, but the phenotype in the other family (F1) was not linked to this locus.

checks.claim: Masotti et al. (2008) performed genome-wide linkage analysis in 2 large families with auriculocondylar syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: we conducted linkage analysis in two large ACS families, F1 and F2
checks.explanation: The abstract also says 'we performed a wide genome search'.

checks.claim: Auriculocondylar syndrome in family F2 showed linkage to 1p21.1-q23.3.
checks.evidence_quote: we observed evidence of linkage to 1p21.1-q23.3 in F2 (LOD max 3.01 at theta=0)

checks.claim: Auriculocondylar syndrome in family F1 was not linked to the 1p21.1-q23.3 locus.
checks.evidence_quote: Interestingly, this locus was not linked to the phenotype segregating in F1.

paragraphs.text: In the 4-generation Brazilian family F1, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) found no pathogenic variants in PLCB4, GNAI3, or EDN1. Linkage analysis assuming autosomal dominant inheritance gave a maximum LOD score of 2.88 (maximum theoretical score, 2.93) in a 17.6-Mb region on chromosome 7. Microsatellite markers narrowed this region to chr7:14395902-28158440 (hg38).

checks.claim: Family F1 with auriculocondylar syndrome is a 4-generation Brazilian family.
checks.evidence_quote: The CNV, which segregated with the disease in a four-generation large Brazilian family

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) used targeted resequencing in affected members of the Brazilian family F1 originally reported by Masotti et al. (2008). They identified a 430-kb tandem duplication (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) that began about 280 kb telomeric to TWIST1 and covered most of the HDAC9 gene. Several shorter HDAC9 isoforms were duplicated in full, whereas the full-length catalytically active isoforms were predicted to be disrupted. The authors amplified the breakpoint and used Sanger sequencing to show that the duplication segregated with the phenotype. No unaffected family member carried it (LOD score 2.88).

checks.evidence_quote: We herein describe a new multigeneration family with 11 affected individuals (F1)
checks.explanation: The abstract confirms that Masotti et al. reported F1. It does not say the family is Brazilian; that detail may be in the full text, which was not supplied.

checks.explanation: One unaffected member was also sequenced.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) also identified 19 patients in the DECIPHER database with copy-number gains in the region. Seven of them had ear malformations and 7 had micrognathia, and most of these duplications included the TWIST1 enhancer eTW6. One patient without features of ARCND had a 179-kb duplication that lay entirely within the ARCND duplication but did not include the TWIST1 regulatory elements.

checks.claim: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) identified 19 patients in the DECIPHER database with copy-number gains in the ARCND4 duplication region.
checks.evidence_quote: Analysis of CNVs in DECIPHER (https://decipher.sanger.ac.uk/) revealed 19 patients with copy-number gains in the region.

checks.claim: Seven of the 19 DECIPHER patients with copy-number gains in the region had ear malformations.
checks.evidence_quote: Nevertheless, 7 out of 19 have descriptions that include ear malformation among other features

checks.claim: Seven of the 19 DECIPHER patients with copy-number gains in the region had micrognathia.
checks.evidence_quote: Similarly, 7 out of 19 DECIPHER patients presented with micrognathia

checks.claim: Most of the DECIPHER duplications in the region included the TWIST1 enhancer eTW6.
checks.evidence_quote: Similarly, 7 out of 19 DECIPHER patients presented with micrognathia (patient identification: 393911, 393942, 395511, 280316, 2363, 396373 and 394346); these duplications also include eTW6, except for individual 2363.
checks.explanation: Paper reports eTW6 inclusion only for the duplications in patients with ear malformation/micrognathia, not for most of all 19.

checks.claim: One DECIPHER patient without features of ARCND had a 179-kb duplication lying entirely within the ARCND duplication.
checks.evidence_quote: Interestingly, one of the DECIPHER duplications (276644; 179 kb) is enclosed entirely within the ARCND duplicated region; however, this patient does not have ARCND clinical features

checks.evidence_quote: We note that the non-overlapping sequence between patient 276644 and the ARCND duplication includes the aforementioned regulatory TWIST1 elements

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) performed Capture-C from the TWIST1 promoter in human embryonic calvarial mesenchymal cells. The most frequent cis interactions were telomeric to TWIST1, within HDAC9 and the duplicated region. This suggested that the region contains TWIST1 regulatory elements, which would give the duplication a possible pathogenic mechanism.

checks.evidence_quote: For the chromatin template we prepared human mesenchymal cells from human embryonic calvaria

checks.claim: The most frequent cis interactions of the TWIST1 promoter were telomeric to TWIST1, within HDAC9 and the ARCND4 duplicated region.
checks.evidence_quote: The highest frequency of interactions was telomeric of TWIST1, particularly within the HDAC9 gene and the region spanned by the duplication (figure 1A).

checks.claim: Capture-C results suggested that the ARCND4 duplicated region contains TWIST1 regulatory elements.
checks.evidence_quote: This implies that this region contains regulatory elements involved in the control of TWIST1 expression, providing a possible pathogenic mechanism for the duplication.

checks.claim: The presence of TWIST1 regulatory elements in the duplicated region would give the ARCND4 duplication a possible pathogenic mechanism.
checks.evidence_quote: This implies that this region contains regulatory elements involved in the control of TWIST1 expression, providing a possible pathogenic mechanism for the duplication.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) found that neural crest cells derived from patient iPSCs expressed more HDAC9 (3.15-fold) and TWIST1 (2.03-fold) than control cells. The patient cells also showed a 4.3-fold decrease in migration. During osteogenic differentiation, patient mesenchymal cells had lower alkaline phosphatase activity and less matrix mineralization, which the authors interpreted as delayed or impaired osteogenesis.

checks.evidence_quote: However, an increase in HDAC9 (3.15-fold, unpaired t-test p=0.009) and TWIST1 (2.03-fold, unpaired t-test p=0.03) mRNA was observed in the ARCND-iNCC

checks.claim: Neural crest cells derived from ARCND4 patient iPSCs showed a 4.3-fold decrease in migration.
checks.evidence_quote: a significant decrease in migratory capacity of ARCND iNCCs was observed compared with controls (4.3-fold decrease, Student’s t-test, p=0.0009)

checks.claim: During osteogenic differentiation, ARCND4 patient mesenchymal cells had lower alkaline phosphatase activity.
checks.evidence_quote: ALP enzymatic activity was significantly diminished in ARCND-nMSCs after 9 days of osteoinduction

checks.claim: During osteogenic differentiation, ARCND4 patient mesenchymal cells had less matrix mineralization.
checks.evidence_quote: alizarin red staining revealed a subtle decrease in matrix mineralisation in ARCND-nMSCs in comparison with controls

checks.claim: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) interpreted the findings in ARCND4 patient mesenchymal cells as delayed or impaired osteogenesis.
checks.evidence_quote: Together, these results indicate a delay or impairment of osteogenic differentiation.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) studied a nonconsanguineous Brazilian family (F1) with 11 members affected by auriculocondylar syndrome-4 (ARCND4). In affected members they identified a 430,302-bp tandem duplication (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) telomeric to TWIST1 that covered most of the HDAC9 gene. The duplication segregated with the phenotype, and all unaffected family members were negative for it (LOD score 2.88). Neural crest cells derived from patient iPSCs showed increased HDAC9 and TWIST1 expression and reduced migration. Capture-C showed that the duplicated region interacted with the TWIST1 promoter.
